Phase I combined analysis¶

This notebook pools the four available Phase I baseline files and treats all respondents as one analysis population.

Course/source labels are retained only for provenance and data-quality checks; no between-course inference is performed.

Pool and score the four datasets¶

Pooled descriptive statistics and reliability¶

In [3]:
pooled_summary = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        'construct': label,
        'n': df[column].notna().sum(),
        'mean': df[column].mean(),
        'sd': df[column].std(ddof=1),
        'median': df[column].median(),
        'iqr': df[column].quantile(.75) - df[column].quantile(.25),

Interpretation¶

  • Mean overall AI literacy is 3.57 on the original 1–5 scale (SD = 0.42). AI literacy is not standardized in this descriptive table.

  • The SES-index mean is effectively zero by design because all seven SES items are standardized using the pooled 232-person means and SDs after merging, and the item z-scores are then averaged.

  • The SES-index SD is 0.57 rather than 1.00 because it is the mean of seven correlated item z-scores; the composite itself is not re-standardized here. The regression function subsequently standardizes the final SES index and AI outcome when reporting standardized β.

  • SES ingredients have moderate internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.687). This is close to the commonly used 0.70 threshold and is reasonable for a multidimensional SES index construct.

  • AI-literacy items have low internal consistency (α = 0.504). The items appear to cover heterogeneous conceptual-knowledge and ability/confidence domains rather than one interchangeable item set.

SES association with overall AI literacy¶

$$\text{AI literacy} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{SES} + \varepsilon$$

The pooled single linear regression uses HC3 robust standard errors.

Interpretation¶

  • Higher SES is associated with higher overall AI literacy (standardized β = 0.209, HC3 p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.087, 0.330]).

  • The effect is small: SES explains approximately 4.4% of the variance in AI literacy. The Spearman estimate is similar (ρ = 0.215, p = 0.001), suggesting the result is not driven solely by the linear-model scale.

Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)¶

EFA for AI Literacy¶

Two-factor exploratory models are fitted for AI literacy and SES to match the existing Phase I specification.

AI-literacy EFA interpretation¶

  • Bartlett's test is significant and the overall KMO is 0.658, indicating that factor analysis is usable but sampling adequacy is only modest.

  • Three eigenvalues exceed 1, while the theory-guided two-factor solution explains 29.2% of item variance. The retained two-factor structure is therefore plausible but not uniquely determined by the data.

SES EFA interpretation¶

  • Bartlett's test is significant and the KMO is 0.728, providing better support for the SES factor analysis than for the AI-literacy factor analysis.

  • Two eigenvalues exceed 1, and the two retained factors explain 40.0% of the SES-item variance.

  • The two scores summarize related family/institutional and material-resource dimensions.

  • These factor scores are not equal-weighted averages. Each observed SES variable is standardized, then multiplied by the displayed factor-score weight for each dimension. The weighted values are summed for each respondent. With oblimin rotation, the two factors are allowed to correlate.

  • The weights are estimated from the pooled correlation structure using minimum-residual EFA. Their signs and magnitudes determine how strongly each SES variable contributes to each factor score.

Exploratory mediation analysis¶

  • The revised analysis estimates 12 simple mediation models: 2 SES factors × 3 retained mediators × 2 AI-literacy factors.

Conceptual exposure and learning ecology remain in the scored dataset but are excluded from mediation, network, and hierarchical models.

  • Bootstrap confidence intervals use 5,000 resamples.

  • Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) false-discovery-rate correction is the only multiplicity adjustment used.

In [7]:
retained_mediator_names = ['practical_ai_use', 'language_load', 'epistemic_stance']
retained_mediators = [f'{name}_score' for name in retained_mediator_names]
mediator_reliability = mediator_reliability_table(df, mediator_map)
mediator_reliability = mediator_reliability[
    mediator_reliability['mediator'].isin(retained_mediator_names)
]
display(mediator_reliability)

df_med = add_mediator_composites(df, mediator_map)
df_analysis = add_ses_ai_factor_scores(
    df_base=df_med, ai_df=df, ai_items=ai_efa_items, ai_fa=ai_fa,
    ses_df=df_ses, ses_items=ses_efa_items, ses_fa=ses_fa,
)
df_analysis.to_csv('datasets/df_analysis_phase_I_combined.csv', index=False)

mediation_results = run_all_simple_mediations(

Interpretation¶

  • The language-load questions show good consistency (α = 0.737), so they provide the clearest measurement among the three retained mediators.

  • The most promising pattern suggests that students with stronger scores on the first SES dimension may gain AI confidence partly through more practical AI use. However, this pattern does not meet the BH threshold after checking all 12 pathways, so it should guide future data collection rather than be presented as a confirmed mechanism.

  • In plain language, the current sample does not yet distinguish which of the three experiences carries the SES difference into AI literacy. The direct associations and network patterns below are clearer than the indirect pathways.

Partial-correlation network¶

  • Edges represent conditional associations after controlling for every other variable in the network.

  • Benjamini-Hochberg FDR is the primary exploratory correction. Edges are not causal effects.

In [8]:
analysis_vars = [
    'ses_index', 'practical_ai_use_score', 'language_load_score',
    'epistemic_stance_score', 'ai_factor1_score', 'ai_factor2_score',

Interpretation¶

  • Seven relationships remain clear after BH correction.

  • Students who experience more language difficulty tend to show lower AI understanding and lower AI confidence. This makes language accessibility a practical target for course design.

  • Students with a stronger epistemic stance—more active evaluation of information and knowledge—tend to show higher AI understanding and confidence. Practical AI use also goes together with higher AI confidence and a stronger epistemic stance.

  • Practical AI use also rises with language load. One plausible interpretation is that students facing greater language demands may turn to AI tools more often; the cross-sectional data cannot determine the direction.

  • The graph maps relationships after accounting for the other included variables. It shows which factors travel together, but it does not prove that one causes another.

Hierarchical regression¶

Model 1 contains the two SES factors; Model 2 adds the three retained mediators; Model 3 adds one exploratory practical-AI-use × epistemic-stance interaction. This interaction follows the two strongest positive candidate pathways in the mediation and network results. Both block and coefficient tests use Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, with HC3 standard errors for coefficients.

In [9]:
practical_z = (
    df_analysis['practical_ai_use_score']
    - df_analysis['practical_ai_use_score'].mean()
) / df_analysis['practical_ai_use_score'].std(ddof=0)
epistemic_z = (
    df_analysis['epistemic_stance_score']
    - df_analysis['epistemic_stance_score'].mean()
) / df_analysis['epistemic_stance_score'].std(ddof=0)
df_analysis['practical_x_epistemic'] = practical_z * epistemic_z

Interpretation¶

  • For AI understanding, students report lower scores when language demands are heavier (β = -0.320) and higher scores when they more actively evaluate information and knowledge (β = 0.258). These two relationships remain clear after accounting for SES, practical AI use, and BH correction.

  • For AI confidence, the final model identifies four independent relationships after BH correction: SES factor 2 (β = 0.166), practical AI use (β = 0.187), and epistemic stance (β = 0.219) relate to higher confidence, while language load relates to lower confidence (β = -0.204). This points to two actionable levers—hands-on AI practice and support for evaluating information—and one barrier, language difficulty. The remaining SES coefficient indicates that these experiences do not fully account for the socioeconomic confidence gap.

  • Adding practical AI use × epistemic stance raises explained variance in AI confidence from 15.6% to 20.8% (ΔR² = 0.052; BH-adjusted block p < 0.001). The plotted negative interaction suggests that practical experience may relate most strongly to confidence among students with lower epistemic-stance scores. However, the HC3 interaction coefficient itself is only suggestive (β = -0.231, raw p = 0.079, BH p = 0.095), so this pattern needs confirmation rather than a firm causal claim.

  • For the project's bridging question, these Phase I results identify possible intervention targets but do not show that an intervention closes an SES gap. Phase II must test whether change over time differs by SES, ideally through an SES × intervention/time term.

AI literacy by prior AI-course experience¶

Compares respondents who reported prior AI-related coursework with those who did not.

  • Examines overall AI literacy, AI understanding, AI confidence, and the three retained mediators: practical AI use, language load, and epistemic stance.

  • Each comparison uses a two-sided Welch t-test and Cohen's d. Benjamini–Hochberg correction controls the false discovery rate across the six tests.

  • For the three mediators, two one-sided tests (TOST) additionally assess practical equivalence within Cohen's d = ±0.20, with BH correction across those three equivalence tests.

In [10]:
prior_course_counts = pd.crosstab(
    df_analysis['source_dataset'],
    df_analysis['ai_course_taken_num'].map({0: 'No', 1: 'Yes'}),
    margins=True,
)
course_aspects = {
    'ai_lit_score': 'Overall AI literacy',
    'ai_factor1_score': 'AI understanding',
    'ai_factor2_score': 'AI confidence',
    'practical_ai_use_score': 'Practical AI use',
    'language_load_score': 'Language load',
    'epistemic_stance_score': 'Epistemic stance',
}
course_descriptive_parts = []
course_test_parts = []
for score_col, aspect in course_aspects.items():
    descriptive, comparison = compare_ai_literacy_by_prior_course(
        df_analysis, score_col=score_col
    )
    descriptive.insert(0, 'aspect', aspect)
    comparison.insert(0, 'aspect', aspect)
    course_descriptive_parts.append(descriptive)
    course_test_parts.append(comparison)

prior_course_descriptive = pd.concat(course_descriptive_parts, ignore_index=True)
prior_course_tests = pd.concat(course_test_parts, ignore_index=True)
prior_course_tests['p_bh'] = multipletests(
    prior_course_tests['p_value_two_sided'], method='fdr_bh'
)[1]
prior_course_tests['significant_bh'] = prior_course_tests['p_bh'] < .05
course_group_means = (
    prior_course_descriptive
    .pivot(index='aspect', columns='prior_ai_course', values='mean')
    .rename(columns={'No': 'mean_no_prior_course', 'Yes': 'mean_prior_course'})
    .reset_index()
)
prior_course_results = course_group_means.merge(
    prior_course_tests[[
        'aspect', 'mean_difference_yes_minus_no', 'cohen_d', 'p_value_two_sided',
        'p_bh', 'significant_bh',
    ]],
    on='aspect', how='left',
)

# A non-significant difference is not evidence that groups are identical.
# TOST checks whether mediator differences are small enough to fall within
# a prespecified equivalence interval of Cohen's d = -0.20 to +0.20.
selected_mediator_aspects = {
    'Practical AI use': 'practical_ai_use_score',
    'Language load': 'language_load_score',
    'Epistemic stance': 'epistemic_stance_score',
}
equivalence_bound_d = 0.20
equivalence_rows = []
for aspect, score_col in selected_mediator_aspects.items():
    prior = df_analysis.loc[
        df_analysis['ai_course_taken_num'].eq(1), score_col
    ].dropna()
    no_prior = df_analysis.loc[
        df_analysis['ai_course_taken_num'].eq(0), score_col
    ].dropna()
    pooled_sd = np.sqrt(
        ((len(prior) - 1) * prior.var(ddof=1)
         + (len(no_prior) - 1) * no_prior.var(ddof=1))
        / (len(prior) + len(no_prior) - 2)
    )
    raw_bound = equivalence_bound_d * pooled_sd
    tost_p, _, _ = ttost_ind(
        prior, no_prior, -raw_bound, raw_bound, usevar='unequal'
    )
    equivalence_rows.append({
        'aspect': aspect,
        'equivalence_bound_d': equivalence_bound_d,
        'equivalence_bound_raw': raw_bound,
        'p_tost': tost_p,
    })
mediator_equivalence = pd.DataFrame(equivalence_rows)
mediator_equivalence['p_tost_bh'] = multipletests(
    mediator_equivalence['p_tost'], method='fdr_bh'
)[1]
mediator_equivalence['equivalent_within_d_0_20'] = (
    mediator_equivalence['p_tost_bh'] < .05
)
prior_course_results = prior_course_results.merge(
    mediator_equivalence, on='aspect', how='left'
)
mediator_course_results = prior_course_results[
    prior_course_results['aspect'].isin(selected_mediator_aspects)
].copy()
prior_course_results.to_csv(
    'datasets/prior_course_comparisons_phase_I_combined.csv', index=False
)
display(prior_course_counts)
display(prior_course_results)
display(mediator_course_results)

course_plot = df_analysis[
    ['ai_course_taken_num'] + list(course_aspects)
].melt(
    id_vars='ai_course_taken_num', var_name='measure', value_name='score'
).dropna()
course_plot['Prior AI-related course'] = course_plot['ai_course_taken_num'].map(
    {0: 'No', 1: 'Yes'}
)
course_plot['aspect'] = course_plot['measure'].map(course_aspects)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 9))
for ax, aspect in zip(axes.flat, course_aspects.values()):
    sub = course_plot[course_plot['aspect'] == aspect]
    sns.boxplot(
        data=sub, x='Prior AI-related course', y='score',
        order=['No', 'Yes'], width=.5, showfliers=False, ax=ax,
    )
    sns.stripplot(
        data=sub, x='Prior AI-related course', y='score',
        order=['No', 'Yes'], color='black', alpha=.35, jitter=.18, size=3, ax=ax,
    )
    ax.set_title(aspect)
    ax.set_xlabel('Prior AI-related HKU course')
    ax.set_ylabel('Score')
fig.suptitle('Detailed comparison by prior AI-course experience', y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation¶

  • Students with and without prior AI coursework have similar observed means on all three retained mediators.

  • A non-significant difference does not establish that two groups are identical. Using the stricter TOST equivalence analysis, none of the three mediators is confirmed equivalent within a small-effect interval of d = ±0.20 after BH correction. The present data are therefore inconclusive: they show no clear group differences, but they also do not prove practical equality.

Results summary for brief reporting¶

  • The pooled dataset contains 232 unique respondents: 141 from the 2025 exports and 91 from the 2026 exports, combining the 1111, 1201, and 1204 cohorts.

  • Students from higher-SES backgrounds report higher overall AI literacy. The relationship is small but clear (standardized β = 0.209, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.087, 0.330]) and explains 4.4% of the variation among students.

  • SES dimension reduction: Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) reduced the 7 SES indicators to 2 related dimensions that together explain 40.0% of their shared variation (KMO = 0.728). The dimensions are regression-weighted EFA factor scores, rather than simple or equally weighted averages:

    1. SES 1 — Parental educational capital: this dimension is driven mainly by parent/caregiver education, especially the second reported parent/caregiver's education in this sample.

    2. SES 2 — Household material resources: this dimension combines household income, fewer financial constraints, living space per person, and housing type.

  • The BH-corrected Network Analysis highlights 7 clear relationships:

    1. Students who experience greater language difficulty tend to report lower AI understanding and confidence. Language accessibility may therefore be one practical barrier to closing the AI-literacy gap.

    2. Students with a higher epistemic-stance score tend to report better AI understanding and greater confidence. This pattern suggests that becoming comfortable with critically assessing information may support both knowing how AI works and feeling able to use it.

    3. More practical AI use is connected with greater confidence and a higher epistemic-stance score. Hands-on experience may therefore build confidence while giving students more opportunities to practise evaluating AI-related information.

  • The Resampled Mediation Analysis identifies 2 nominal candidate pathways and 1 near-threshold candidate, all beginning with SES 1 (parental educational capital):

    1. Parental educational capital → practical AI use → AI confidence: students from more highly educated family backgrounds tended to have more hands-on AI experience, and students with more hands-on experience tended to feel more confident using AI. Practical opportunities may therefore be one way that family educational advantage is translated into AI confidence (indirect effect = 0.029, 95% bootstrap CI [0.001, 0.076], raw p = 0.032).

    2. Parental educational capital → epistemic stance → AI understanding: students from more highly educated family backgrounds tended to report a stronger evaluative approach to information, which in turn was linked with better AI understanding. This suggests that family educational resources may help cultivate ways of judging information that support learning about AI (indirect effect = 0.039, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.081], raw p = 0.050).

    3. Near-threshold pathway to AI confidence: the same evaluative approach may also help convert parental educational advantage into greater AI confidence, although this signal is slightly less certain (indirect effect = 0.034, 95% CI [-0.0001, 0.090], raw p = 0.052).

    These are exploratory clues about possible mechanisms, not confirmed causal pathways: all three have BH-adjusted p = 0.206. The pattern specifically concerns parental educational capital (SES 1), rather than household material resources (SES 2).

  • The Hierarchical Models sharpen the intervention picture:

    1. Language difficulty is linked with lower AI understanding and confidence, suggesting that clearer or more accessible language could reduce a barrier faced by some students.

    2. Epistemic stance is linked with both better understanding and greater confidence, suggesting that activities that practise questioning and assessing information may support both outcomes.

    3. Practical AI use is linked with greater confidence. However, household material resources (SES 2) remain related to confidence even after the three mediators are included, so differences in language load, practical use, and epistemic stance do not fully account for the resource-related confidence gap.

  • The exploratory practical-AI-use × epistemic-stance model raises explained AI-confidence variance from 15.6% to 20.8%.

    The interaction plot suggests that hands-on AI practice may matter most for students with lower epistemic stance, but the robust interaction coefficient does not pass BH correction.
